18925.text: *satar* H5641, hide (75 no-seat) | Psa 143:7 "my spirit fails! Hide not your face"; Psa 88:14 soul; Psa 104:29 "they are dismayed … breath"; Psa 10:11 heart | God hiding his face. The seat is the human recipient's: Psa 13:1 (13:2 "sorrow in my heart"); Psa 30:7 "you hid your face; I was dismayed"; Psa 44:24; 69:17; 102:2; Isa 8:17 ("I will wait … and I will hope in him"); Isa 54:8; 59:2; 64:7; Mic 3:4; Deu 31:17 | Physical hiding (David 1Sa 20, 23, 26; Jeremiah and Baruch Jer 36): outward, with inner being behind the act at most. 19035.text: The passage. *"their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'"* (9:3). He hired *"worthless and reckless fellows"* with silver from the house of Baal-berith (9:4). He *"killed his brothers … seventy men, on one stone"* (9:5).

19217.text: Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". New in v3: when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in the heart and spirit. The seat is where the cleansing is to happen. The requests go on: "Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11), then "uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12). The face hidden from the sin (51:9) is set against the presence not withdrawn from the person (51:11). Between them stand two spirits: God's, which is not to be taken away, and the human's, which is to be renewed and made willing.; New in v3: Psa 102:2 ("Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress") → 102:4 "My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread". The distress of 102:2 is a withered heart, and it reaches the body: the sufferer forgets to eat. It is the same movement as Psa 44:25 ("our belly clings to the ground").; New in v3: Psa 27:9 ← 27:8 "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek.'" The heart seeks the face one verse before it asks that the face not be hidden. The petition "Hide not your face" (27:9) is the voice of a heart already turned toward the face. What hiddenness would cut off is the heart's own seeking.; New in v3: Psa 69:17 → 69:20 "Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none". The "distress" of 69:17 is named three verses later as a broken heart that finds no comforter. The hidden face of 69:17 and the absent human pity of 69:20 are the same lack, felt from God and from people. In between, the petition names the soul: "Draw near to my soul, redeem me" (69:18). The opposite of the hidden face is God drawing near to the soul.; New in v3, the resolution in the heart: Psa 22:24 ("he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard") → 22:26 "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord! May your hearts live forever!" When the face is not hidden, the outcome lands in hearts that live. It is the reverse of the withered heart that forgets to eat (Psa 102:4): here the afflicted eat, and the hearts live.

19224.text: (a) Concealing one's own wrong. Each case has its own sequence: Achan: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Jos 7:21); Joshua: "tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (7:19); Achan: "Truly I have sinned" (7:20); "behold, it was hidden in his tent" (7:22); Seeing, coveting, taking, hiding, being demanded to disclose, confessing, being found.; Moses: "He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand" (Exo 2:12). When the deed surfaces: "Moses was afraid, and thought, 'Surely the thing is known'" (2:14). Concealment fails, and fear follows.; The hidden adultery: "it is hidden from the eyes of her husband" (Num 5:13). The next verse: "the spirit of jealousy comes over him" (5:14). Where a deed is hidden, suspicion grows in the other person.; Job's denial: "if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart [*chob*, bosom], because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence" (Job 31:33–34). The verse names the motive for concealing sin: fear of social contempt. Job denies he acted on it.; The lepers: they hid the plunder (2Ki 7:8), then "said to one another, 'We are not doing right … If we are silent … punishment will overtake us'" (7:9). Conscience reverses concealment into telling.; Concealment as savouring: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth" (Job 20:12–13). The hidden sin is kept because it is enjoyed.; Not hiding at all: "the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it" (Isa 3:9). The face discloses: shamelessness.

19230.text: How it co-exists. Fear is the most frequent companion, on both sides: fear drives concealment (Job 31:34; Mat 25:25), or follows its failure (Exo 2:14); fear blocks disclosure until it is overcome (1Sa 3:15–18); Joy (Mat 13:44), enjoyment of sin (Job 20:12–13) and conscience (2Ki 7:9) are the other companions.

19231.text: Seat.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 40:10 "I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart". Batch A v3 §6 ("The heart can conceal or not"). The heart is the place where a word could be kept back, and the verse says it was not.; In the verse, the offender's own self: Isa 3:9 "they have brought evil on themselves [*their nephesh*]". Batch D v2 §2.3 ("Evil against one's own soul"). Seat-sense: *nephesh* is here the self, reflexively, and it passes the check in that sense. New in v3: the verse holds the phenomenon and its outcome together. The face does *not* conceal ("they do not hide it"), and the evil disclosed comes back on the self that disclosed it. Shamelessness is not a safe disclosure.; In the next verse, the other party's (genuine): Num 5:13 → 5:14 "the spirit of jealousy comes over him". The deed is hidden in the wife; the seat that registers it is the husband's spirit (v2).; A seat outside M47: Job 31:33 *chob*, "bosom", where the iniquity would be hidden (v1 §3 item 6; not an M47 word).; In the passage, the bearer's own — new in v3: Job 6:10 ("This would be my comfort … for I have not denied the words of the Holy One") is flanked by two uses of *nephesh*: "My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me" (6:7). *Nephesh* is appetite here. The sense passes the check only as bodily desire, and it has turned to loathing.; "What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?" (6:11). *Nephesh* is inside the English "be patient", literally "lengthen my soul". It is genuine, and the soul cannot endure.; Job's one comfort, that he has not concealed God's words, stands between an appetite that loathes and a soul that can no longer wait. Not concealing is the one thing left intact.; Spurious context link: 2Sa 14:18 → 14:19 "As surely as you live [*nephesh*]" is an oath formula. Batch G v3 §4 read the formula as "the soul as what one swears by". It says nothing of the disclosure.; Whose seat, strand (b) and (e): none. The disclosures of Samuel, the kings' demands, the treasure-finder's joy and the servant's fear are all carried by speech and act, not by a seat word.

19250.text: (e) Cares that choke. The sower parable: "the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word" (Mat 13:22); "the cares of the world … enter in and choke the word" (Mar 4:19); "as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life" (Luk 8:14); "lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life" (Luk 21:34).; Where from: outside ("enter in").; What it does: it acts on the word already received. It chokes it and weighs down the heart.; Co-exists with riches, pleasures and drunkenness.; Leads to: "it proves unfruitful"; "that day come upon you suddenly like a trap".

19256.text: Strand (b), a divine Spirit replaces the anxious speaker's own seat. Mat 10:19 → 10:20 "it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you". Batch E v2 §1.6 ("The Spirit speaks through the person"). The anxiety about what to say is answered by another's Spirit in the speaker's place. The Luke parallel runs the same way: Luk 12:11 → 12:12 "for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say". Luke gives the answer as teaching: the Spirit supplies the knowing that the anxiety lacked.; Strand (e), the choked hearer is set between two hearts — new in v3. Luk 8:14 (the thorns) stands between "the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts" (8:12) and "hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience" (8:15). The cares act on a heart where the word has been sown, and the contrast the passage draws is with a good heart that holds the word fast. Mat 13:22 ← 13:19 "snatches away what has been sown in his heart" is the same frame (v1 §2 *merimna* row).; The man who is not anxious. Jer 17:8 is framed by "whose heart turns away from the Lord" (17:5), and by "The heart is deceitful … I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (17:9–10) (v1 §2 *de'agah* row). The unanxious tree stands between two statements about the heart.; Strand (g), a neighbouring oracle's heart. Jer 49:23 (Hamath and Arpad "melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea") follows 49:22, the end of the oracle against Edom: "the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains". The party is different: Edom in 49:22, the cities of Damascus in 49:23. So the seat does not belong to the anxious ones of 49:23. What the two oracles share is the same collapse under bad news. It is stated as a heart in labour for Edom's warriors, and as melting and a troubled sea for Hamath. It is recorded as a parallel, not as the seat of 49:23.; Spurious context link: Jer 38:19 → 38:17 "your life shall be spared". *Nephesh* is bodily life here: the life Zedekiah fears to lose. It names what the dread is about, not a seat.

19403.text: Joshua 24:15 — "choose this day whom you will serve": Joshua does not open with the choice. He opens with eleven verses in which the Lord speaks of what *he* did: *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"*; *"I brought you out"*; *"I gave them into your hand"*; *"it was not by your sword or by your bow"* (v3–12); The recital starts where the people's story started: *"your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates … and they served other gods"* (v2). Before Israel ever chose, the Lord had already taken Abraham out from among those gods. The choice put to the people at Shechem comes at the end of that history, not at the start of it.; The choice is not whether to serve. Serving is taken for granted: the fathers served gods beyond the River, and the Amorites serve the gods of the land. The only question is *whom*. So the choosing is a choice of master.; It begins in the eyes: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"*. Joshua treats the people's own view of what is good and evil as where the choice starts, and he leaves it open to them. He even names the alternatives for them. Then he makes his own choice in front of them, before they answer: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord."*; The people choose from memory: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us … up from the land of Egypt, … and who did those great signs in our sight"* (v17). Their choosing rests on what they saw.; Joshua's reply is not what a speaker would say if he only wanted agreement: *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God"* (v19). Choosing and being able to carry the choice out are not the same thing, and Joshua says so plainly. The people insist, *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (v21).; At that point the choice turns back on the one who made it: *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (v22). Once spoken, a choice becomes a testimony the chooser will be held to.; It also exposes what is still in the house: *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (v23). The people have just chosen the Lord, yet the foreign gods are still among them. So the choice spoken with the mouth has to be followed by two things: putting something away; an inner turning, the heart inclined (H5186, "to stretch, bend")

19545.text: Outcome: The choice binds them as its own witness: *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"*; *"We are witnesses"* (v22).; It calls for an inner act: *"put away the foreign gods … and incline your heart to the Lord"* (v23).; *"his voice we will obey"* (v24). A covenant, statutes and rules are made, and a stone is set up as *"a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God"* (v25–27).; The warning is part of the outcome: *"If you forsake the Lord … he will turn and do you harm"* (v20).

19673.text: The choice is held, not just made. It is set between keeping and holding fast (Isa 56:2, 4, 6), and between eyes turned to the Lord and waiting (Psa 25:15, 21). This sits with the test readings: the heart inclined after the choice (Jos 24:23), and clinging to the testimonies (Psa 119:31).

Verse 7, about the heart, lies outside the pull.; David: "who chose me above your father … to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the Lord —and I will celebrate before the Lord" (2Sa 6:21); "He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds" (Psa 78:70); "I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant" (Psa 89:3); Solomon "whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great" (1Ch 29:1). Being chosen is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10).; Sonship: "I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father" (1Ch 28:6); Saul is named "the chosen of the Lord" by the Gibeonites, in the demand for his sons (2Sa 21:6).

20281.text: What Solomon asks of God in return: *"forgive your people … and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive"* (v50). At the end he prays for the heart once more: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (v58), and *"Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the Lord our God"* (v61). The day ends with the people going home *"joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown"* (v66).

20389.text: Psalm 32:2: "the man against whom the Lord counts no iniquity": > Q1 citation: ❗ Needs attention. Ch 6: "The righteous man is the one 'in whose spirit there is no deceit'". The psalm's man is the forgiven one: "whose transgression is forgiven" (v1), against whom the Lord counts no iniquity (v2). The no-deceit sits beside his confession: "I did not cover my iniquity" (v5). Ch 6 makes it a quality of the righteous, not of the one who confessed. Ch 9 ("It has or lacks 'deceit'") is accurate.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: corroborates and adds. Corroborates 10.9 *God reckons, and faith reckons*, through Rom 4:8, which quotes this verse. New: the not counting comes after confession, following silence (vv3–5). Shimei asks the same of David with the same word (2Sa 19:19).; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M14 deceit (H7423A): yes, for 10.11 *Hiding and disclosing*: no deceit stands with not covering iniquity (v5). M56 iniquity and M80 blessed: no.; *"Blessed is the man against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit"* (v2). Then: *"when I kept silent, my bones wasted away"* (v3); *"I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin"* (v5); "Counts" is H2803H, God's reckoning.

20456.text: 4.2 What thoughts are: Inner speech. 21 of the rows (H0559, *ʾāmar*, "to say") are places where the Hebrew says "he *said*" and the ESV renders it "he thought," as in 1 Samuel 18:11: "Saul thought, 'I will pin David…'" The Greek *dialogismos* (G1261) and *logismos* (G3053) are also built on *logos*, "word" [lexical]. In these texts, to think is to speak inwardly. *Caveat:* how many rows show this depends on the ESV's choices.; Devising or planning. H4284 *maḥăšāvāh* (from H2803 *ḥāšav*, "to devise"). These thoughts are designs with a direction. They can be just (Proverbs 12:5), evil (Isaiah 59:7), or God's own plan (Micah 4:12). Because they point somewhere, they can be judged, and they can be abandoned (Isaiah 55:7).; Likening, or interpreting. H1819 *dāmāh* ("to resemble") is used in Psalm 50:21: "you thought that I was one like yourself." Many rows record thoughts that were wrong: Genesis 38:15, Mark 6:49, Luke 24:37, Matthew 20:10, Acts 12:9, Judges 3:24 and 2 Kings 5:11. So a thought is a reading of reality, not reality itself.; Something that grows and matures. 1 Corinthians 13:11: "I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways."; Transient, yet weighty. Human thoughts are "but a breath" (Psalm 94:11) and "futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20). Yet God weighs them (Proverbs 15:26), and before the flood they were the measure of human wickedness (Genesis 6:5). God's thoughts, by contrast, are "very deep" (Psalm 92:5), "vast" (Psalm 139:17) and "higher" (Isaiah 55:8–9).
